records.title: API Reference
records.description: Endpoints, response shapes and errors for the Provd API.

records.title: Authentication
records.description: Access, rate limits and API keys.
records.content:
## Public endpoints

Reading ratings (`GET /protocols`, `GET /protocols/{slug}`), scanning a contract (`POST /scan`) and requesting early access (`POST /early-access`) need no authentication.

Public endpoints are rate-limited per client. When you exceed the limit the API responds with `429 Too Many Requests`; wait and retry with backoff.

## API keys

Watchlists, webhooks and higher limits are part of the Pro and Protocol plans, currently in early access. Keys are issued to design partners directly. [Request early access](/early-access) and tell us what you want to monitor.

## Good practice

- Treat scan results as a point-in-time read. Use the `checked_at` timestamp when you store them.
- Cache `GET /protocols` responses; ratings are regenerated periodically, not on every request.
- Never put an API key in client-side code once you have one.

records.title: Changelog
records.content:
## 2026-10-02

- Provd is now security-posture monitoring for cross-chain protocols. First coverage: LayerZero V2 OApps and OFTs on Ethereum.
- New public API: `GET /api/v1/protocols`, `GET /api/v1/protocols/{slug}`, `POST /api/v1/scan`, `POST /api/v1/early-access`.
- Published the rating [methodology](/methodology) and our first research note, [Kelp DAO: the exploited route ran on one verifier for 381 days](/blog/kelp-dao-381-days).
- Previous APIs and documentation have been retired.

records.title: Quickstart
records.description: Read a protocol's rating or scan a contract with the Provd API.
records.content:
## Overview

The Provd API returns the same data the website shows: ratings for monitored protocols, and on-demand scans of any LayerZero V2 OApp or OFT on Ethereum. All responses are JSON. The public endpoints need no API key.

Base URL:

```
https://<api-host>/api/v1
```

During early access, ask us for the production host at [hello@provd.tech](mailto:hello@provd.tech). For local development the default is `http://localhost:8000`.

## 1. List rated protocols

```bash
curl -s https://<api-host>/api/v1/protocols
```

Returns a `ProtocolList`: a `generated_at` timestamp and an `items` array with each protocol's grade, score, risk level, single-verifier route count and top findings.

## 2. Get one protocol in full

```bash
curl -s https://<api-host>/api/v1/protocols/<slug>
```

Returns a `ProtocolDetail`: everything in the summary plus every route (`pathways`), the owner and delegate (`admin`), all findings with evidence, and the change history.

## 3. Scan a contract

```bash
curl -s -X POST https://<api-host>/api/v1/scan \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"chain": "ethereum", "address": "0x0000000000000000000000000000000000000000"}'
```

Replace the address with the OApp or OFT you want to check. The scan reads the contract's current configuration over public RPC and returns a `Posture`. Large contracts with many routes can take up to a minute.

## Reading the result

- `grade` (A–F) and `score` (0–100) follow the [methodology](/methodology).
- `single_verifier_pathways` / `pathways_total` is the quickest signal: how many routes accept a message attested by only one verifier.
- Each entry in `findings` carries a `rule_id`, a severity, the affected route eids and `evidence` with links to the on-chain source.

See the [API reference](/docs/api-reference) for every field and error.

records.title: Kelp DAO: the exploited route ran on one verifier for 381 days
records.description: We rebuilt the configuration history of Kelp's rsETH adapter from public on-chain data. The exploited route was set to a single verifier on 2025-04-02 and never changed until the exploit.
records.content:
On **2026-04-18 at 17:35:35 UTC** (Ethereum block 24,908,285) an attacker delivered a forged LayerZero message from Unichain to Kelp's rsETH OFT adapter on Ethereum and released **116,500 rsETH (~$292M)**.

Public accounts of the root cause disagreed. One analysis said the adapter was *deployed* with a single verifier; another said it had been *downgraded* from 2-of-2 to 1-of-1. We rebuilt the adapter's configuration history from public on-chain data to see which was right.

## Summary

- The exploited route (Unichain, eid 30320 → Ethereum) accepted messages attested by **one required verifier — the LayerZero Labs DVN — and no optional verifiers**.
- That setting was made on **2025-04-02 08:14 UTC**, **381 days before the exploit**, and was not changed again before it.
- At the time of the exploit, **24 of the adapter's 26** receive routes were single-verifier.
- The Unichain setting was made by a **single private key (EOA)** that held the adapter's LayerZero delegate role — the account that can change its verifier configuration — from 2025-01-02 to 2025-08-25. It was not the protocol's multisig.
- The widely reported **2-of-2 → 1-of-1 downgrade was real, but it happened on 2024-03-21 — 758 days before the exploit** — and on the Blast and Mode routes, not on Unichain.

Both public accounts were partly right. There was a downgrade, two years earlier; the exploited route itself was never configured with more than one verifier.

Every one of these settings was public and readable on-chain the whole time. A monitor reading them would have flagged the exploited route the day it was opened.

## Timeline

| Date (UTC) | Event |
|---|---|
| 2024-03-15 | The deployer key (an EOA) controls the adapter's verifier configuration. |
| 2024-03-16 | Manta route configured with 2 required verifiers (LayerZero Labs, Polyhedra zkBridge). |
| 2024-03-19 | Blast and Mode routes configured with 2 required verifiers (LayerZero Labs, Polyhedra zkBridge). |
| 2024-03-21 | Blast and Mode reduced to 1 required verifier (LayerZero Labs). This is the "2-of-2 → 1-of-1 downgrade" — 758 days before the exploit. |
| 2024-03-25 → 2024-12-17 | Ten more routes opened with a single verifier by the deployer key. |
| 2025-01-02 | The delegate role moves to a second EOA, `0xCF7b…5662`. |
| 2025-01-24 → 2025-08-18 | Routes opened by this EOA: Bera, Sonic, Hyperliquid, Unichain, TAC and Avalanche with a single verifier; Movement with 2 required verifiers. |
| **2025-04-02 08:14** | **Unichain route (eid 30320) set to 1 required verifier (LayerZero Labs), 0 optional.** Tx `0x2d48d9331d…`. |
| 2025-08-25 | The delegate role moves to a 3-of-6 Safe. |
| 2025-09-15 → 2026-04-01 | Six more routes opened with a single verifier by the Safe: Ink, Plasma, Stable, MegaETH, Mantle, Monad. |
| **2026-04-18 17:35** | **Forged message from Unichain delivered; 116,500 rsETH released.** |
| 2026-04-23 | All 23 active receive routes reconfigured to 4 required verifiers (Horizen, LayerZero Labs, Canary, Nethermind). |
| 2026-06-15 | All peers removed (bridge routes closed). |

## Configuration at the time of the exploit

The adapter had 26 configured receive routes on Ethereum. The last configuration change before the exploit for each one:

| Source chain | eid | Required verifiers | Verifier(s) | Set on | Set by |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Manta | 30217 | 2 | LayerZero Labs, Polyhedra zkBridge | 2024-03-16 | Deployer EOA |
| Blast | 30243 | 1 | LayerZero Labs | 2024-03-21 | Deployer EOA |
| Mode | 30260 | 1 | LayerZero Labs | 2024-03-21 | Deployer EOA |
| Base | 30184 | 1 | LayerZero Labs | 2024-03-25 | Deployer EOA |
| Scroll | 30214 | 1 | LayerZero Labs | 2024-03-25 | Deployer EOA |
| Arbitrum | 30110 | 1 | LayerZero Labs | 2024-04-01 | Deployer EOA |
| Optimism | 30111 | 1 | LayerZero Labs | 2024-04-01 | Deployer EOA |
| Linea | 30183 | 1 | LayerZero Labs | 2024-04-15 | Deployer EOA |
| X Layer | 30274 | 1 | LayerZero Labs | 2024-05-09 | Deployer EOA |
| zkSync Era | 30165 | 1 | LayerZero Labs | 2024-05-16 | Deployer EOA |
| Zircuit | 30303 | 1 | LayerZero Labs | 2024-09-11 | Deployer EOA |
| Hemi | 30329 | 1 | LayerZero Labs | 2024-12-17 | Deployer EOA |
| Swell | 30335 | 1 | LayerZero Labs | 2024-12-17 | Deployer EOA |
| Bera | 30362 | 1 | LayerZero Labs | 2025-01-24 | Delegate EOA |
| Sonic | 30332 | 1 | LayerZero Labs | 2025-03-04 | Delegate EOA |
| Hyperliquid | 30367 | 1 | LayerZero Labs | 2025-03-28 | Delegate EOA |
| **Unichain** | **30320** | **1** | **LayerZero Labs** | **2025-04-02** | **Delegate EOA** |
| Movement | 30325 | 2 | LayerZero Labs, Nethermind | 2025-04-15 | Delegate EOA |
| TAC | 30377 | 1 | LayerZero Labs | 2025-07-13 | Delegate EOA |
| Avalanche | 30106 | 1 | LayerZero Labs | 2025-08-18 | Delegate EOA |
| Ink | 30339 | 1 | LayerZero Labs | 2025-09-15 | 3-of-6 Safe |
| Plasma | 30383 | 1 | LayerZero Labs | 2025-09-16 | 3-of-6 Safe |
| Stable | 30396 | 1 | LayerZero Labs | 2025-12-10 | 3-of-6 Safe |
| MegaETH | 30398 | 1 | LayerZero Labs | 2025-12-23 | 3-of-6 Safe |
| Mantle | 30181 | 1 | LayerZero Labs | 2026-01-01 | 3-of-6 Safe |
| Monad | 30390 | 1 | LayerZero Labs | 2026-04-01 | 3-of-6 Safe |

None of the routes had optional verifiers. 24 of 26 relied on a single verifier; the two exceptions were Manta and Movement.

## Who could change the configuration

The account that can change an OApp's verifier configuration on the LayerZero endpoint is its *delegate*. For Kelp's adapter that role was held by:

| From | To | Account | Type |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2024-03-15 | 2025-01-02 | `0x1f7A…769b` | EOA (deployer key) |
| 2025-01-02 | 2025-08-25 | `0xCF7b…5662` | EOA |
| 2025-08-25 | — | `0xCbcd…29A1` | Safe, 3-of-6 |

For roughly 20 months the adapter's verifier configuration could be changed by a single private key rather than the protocol's multisig. This point was not covered in the public reporting we reviewed. By the time of the exploit the delegate was the 3-of-6 Safe; the single-key period is a separate configuration risk, and it was also readable on-chain.

## What a configuration monitor would have shown

Under the [Provd methodology](/methodology), the Unichain route matches `LZ-SINGLE-VERIFIER` (critical) from 2025-04-02 onwards, and the delegate account matches `ADM-EOA-DELEGATE` (critical) until 2025-08-25. A change monitor would also have raised `CHG-NEW-ROUTE`, escalated to critical, on the day the Unichain route was configured as single-verifier.

That is a statement about visibility, not prevention. A flag does not stop a forged message; it gives the protocol team, its curators and its insurers the information to act on before one arrives.

## Method

1. Decode the exploit transaction's `PacketDelivered` event to get the source endpoint (eid 30320) and the receiving OApp, `0x85d4…8ef3` (`RSETH_OFTAdapter`).
2. Read `EndpointV2.delegates(oapp)` and the adapter's `setDelegate` history to find the three delegates over time.
3. Decode every `EndpointV2.setConfig` call made by each delegate (Blockscout for the EOAs, the Safe Transaction Service for the Safe) and replay the ULN (config type 2) changes in time order.
4. Cross-check: the current `getConfig` for eid 30320 matches the Safe's 2026-04-23 configuration.
5. Resolve DVN names with LayerZero's public metadata registry.

## Limitation

Free RPC endpoints do not serve historical state, so the configuration at each point in time is reconstructed from configuration transactions rather than read directly with a historical `eth_call`. An archive node can confirm each point directly.

## Reproduce it

Reproduce it: [github.com/MeFerdi/provd-web (research/kelp-2026-04)](https://github.com/MeFerdi/provd-web/tree/main/research/kelp-2026-04). The summary data is in `data/kelp_facts.json`; the replay script rebuilds every decoded configuration change from public sources.

If you find an error, write to [security@provd.tech](mailto:security@provd.tech) and we will correct it publicly.
